title: Holley Sniper 2 & Hyperspark Guide ( plus Vintage Air Wiring)
creator: Kenley's Car Stories
recommendation: A strong technical guide covering two popular classic-car upgrades: Holley Sniper 2/Hyperspark EFI and Vintage Air wiring.
seoTitle: Holley Sniper 2 EFI Install & Wiring Guide — 1971 GTO | Fitzgerald Classics
seoDescription: Watch a complete Holley Sniper 2 and HyperSpark install on a 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 — custom battery cables, fuse block, Vintage Air wiring and a no-start diagnosis — with Dan Fitzgerald's written guide, key steps and takeaways.
guide:
Most EFI conversions don't fail on the fuel injection. They fail on the wiring.

That's why this video from Kenley's Car Stories earned a full page here. It's Episode 5 of his 1971 Pontiac GTO 455 restoration, and in just over two hours Kenley installs a Holley Sniper 2 with a HyperSpark distributor, builds the car's power distribution from scratch, wires in his Vintage Air, and then chases down a no-start that turns out to be his own wiring mistake. He shows all of it, including the mistake. That's the kind of video worth studying.

## What the Video Covers

**Getting the Sniper 2 and HyperSpark in place.** The opening stretch covers mounting the EFI unit, installing the HyperSpark distributor, setting timing to top dead center, and deciding where the Holley controller and modules will live.

**Building wires and power distribution.** Kenley builds his MSD 8mm spark plug wires by hand, makes custom battery cables, and adds an underhood fuse block. Before any of it goes to work, he checks the new cables for continuity and resistance.

**The "Nerd Corner."** My favorite part. Kenley slows down and shows how to diagnose high-resistance terminals with a digital volt-ohm meter. A connection can look perfectly fine and still steal voltage. This segment shows how to prove it with a meter instead of guessing.

**Marrying the new system to the old car.** Rather than ripping out the factory wiring, he simplifies the original engine harness and keeps what the car still needs — oil pressure and temperature. The Vintage Air wiring and firewall bulkhead connector go in during this stretch, along with the heater hoses.

**Fuel delivery.** An in-tank fuel pump install, the tank going back in, fuel filter placement, and the wide-band oxygen sensor the Sniper needs in order to learn.

**First power-up — and a no-start.** Software downloads, firmware updates, and the initial settings all go fine. Then the fuel pump won't run. Kenley works the problem on camera and finds it: a wiring mistake in how the power distribution module and a relay were connected — his own error, shown and explained before he fixes it.

**First start.** The 455 fires for the first time in over four months. He finishes by tidying up the wiring, vacuum-filling the cooling system, and checking timing and idle.

## Key Takeaways

- Test new cables before you trust them. A few minutes with a meter on the bench beats hours of guessing under the hood.
- Keep the factory circuits the car still needs. Simplifying a harness is not the same thing as removing it.
- A no-start is usually one wrong connection, not a bad system. The fix in this video came from methodical checking, not new parts.
- Even experienced builders mis-wire something now and then. What matters is having a process that finds it.

## Tools and Parts in This Build

The featured hardware is the Holley Sniper 2 EFI system with the HyperSpark distributor and controller, hand-built MSD 8mm plug wires, an underhood fuse block, custom battery cables, Vintage Air, and an in-tank fuel pump. The tool doing the quiet hero work, though, is a plain digital multimeter.

If your meter is a bargain-bin special that reads a little differently every time you touch the probes, this is the job that will expose it. The meter I recommend in my Garage is the [Fluke 117 True-RMS Digital Multimeter](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Fluke+117+Digital+Multimeter&tag=fitzgeraldcla-20) — the kind of buy-it-once tool that makes a test like Kenley's high-resistance check worth trusting.

*Disclosure: the Fluke link above is an affiliate link. If you buy through it, Fitzgerald Classics earns a small commission at no extra cost to you.*

## Keep Learning

Wiring a build like this one leans on the same fundamentals I wrote about in [Classic Car Electrical Troubleshooting](/post/classic-car-electrical-troubleshooting) — find the fault before you replace parts. If you're testing components off the car, [Bench Testing Classic-Car Electrical Components](/post/bench-testing-classic-car-electrical-components-without-destroying-them) walks through doing it safely, and [7 Electrical Tools Every Classic-Car Owner Should Have](/post/7-electrical-tools-every-classic-car-owner-should-have) covers the rest of the kit.

Hunting parts for your own project? Browse the [Vintage Parts](/vintage-hard-to-find-parts) page for hard-to-find pieces, and the [Garage](/fitzgerald-classics-garage) for the tools and supplies I recommend. Preserving Americana… one classic car at a time.
